prompt: How does an amino group affect electrophilic aromatic substitution on the ring it is attached to?

choices.text: It is strongly activating and ortho- and para-directing
It is strongly deactivating and meta-directing
choices.why: That describes groups such as –NO2. The amino group donates electrons and strongly activates the ring.

choices.text: It is strongly activating and meta-directing
choices.why: Activating groups such as –NH2 direct ortho and para.

choices.text: It has little effect, because the lone pair stays on nitrogen
choices.why: The amino group is so strongly activating that it's hard to prevent polysubstitution.

explanation: An amino group is strongly activating and ortho- and para-directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution. This high reactivity can be a drawback, because it's often difficult to prevent polysubstitution.

prompt: Aniline reacts with Br2 in water. What is the product?

choices.text: 2,4,6-Tribromoaniline
p-Bromoaniline
choices.why: The amino group is so strongly activating that the reaction can't be stopped at the monobromo stage.

choices.text: m-Bromoaniline
choices.why: The amino group directs ortho and para, and the reaction doesn't stop at one bromine.

choices.text: 3,5-Dibromoaniline
choices.why: Bromines go ortho and para to the amino group, at positions 2, 4, and 6.

explanation: Aniline reacts rapidly with Br2 to give 2,4,6-tribromoaniline in 100% yield. The amino group is so strongly activating that it's not possible to stop at the monobromo stage.

prompt: Why are Friedel–Crafts reactions not successful on aniline?

choices.text: The amino group forms an acid–base complex with the AlCl3 catalyst
The amino group strongly deactivates the ring
choices.why: –NH2 is strongly activating. The problem is that the basic nitrogen ties up the Lewis acid catalyst.

choices.text: AlCl3 oxidizes the amino group to a nitro group
choices.why: AlCl3 isn't an oxidizing agent. It forms an acid–base complex with the amino group, which prevents further reaction.

choices.text: The electrophile replaces the amino group on the ring
choices.why: The amino group stays on the ring. It complexes with AlCl3, and that prevents the reaction.

explanation: Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on amino-substituted benzenes because the amino group forms an acid–base complex with the AlCl3 catalyst, which prevents further reaction. Carrying out the reaction on the corresponding amide overcomes this.

prompt: Why does bromination of an N-arylamide stop cleanly at the monobromo product, when bromination of the free arylamine does not?

choices.text: The amido group is less strongly activating than an amino group
The amido group is meta-directing and deactivating
choices.why: Amido groups are still activating and ortho-, para-directing, just less strongly than amino groups.

choices.text: The acetyl group blocks the para position of the ring
choices.why: The acetyl group is on nitrogen, not on the ring.

choices.text: Amides are more basic than amines and complex the Br2
choices.why: Amido substituents are less basic than amino groups, not more.

explanation: Amido substituents (R–N–C=O) are still activating and ortho-, para-directing, but they are less strongly activating and less basic than amino groups, because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized by the neighboring carbonyl group. Bromination then gives a monobromo product, and hydrolysis with aqueous base frees the amine.

prompt: p-Toluidine (4-methylaniline) is treated with acetic anhydride, then with Br2, and then with NaOH in H2O. What is the product?

choices.text: 2-Bromo-4-methylaniline
2,6-Dibromo-4-methylaniline
choices.why: None of the 2,6-dibrominated product is obtained, because the amido group is only moderately activating.

choices.text: 3-Bromo-4-methylaniline
choices.why: Bromination occurs ortho to the acetamido group, on carbon 2, giving 2-bromo-4-methylaniline after hydrolysis.

choices.text: N-(2-Bromo-4-methylphenyl)acetamide
choices.why: That is the intermediate. The final NaOH and H2O step hydrolyzes the amide to the free amine.

explanation: Acetylation gives N-(p-tolyl)acetamide; bromination occurs ortho to the moderately activating amido group; and hydrolysis gives 2-bromo-4-methylaniline. None of the 2,6-dibrominated product is obtained.

prompt: What percentage yield of 2-bromo-4-methylaniline does the section report for the acetylation, bromination, and hydrolysis sequence starting from p-toluidine?
explanation: p-Toluidine is acetylated with acetic anhydride, the amide is brominated, and the amide is hydrolyzed with NaOH in water, giving 2-bromo-4-methylaniline in 79% yield. None of the 2,6-dibrominated product is obtained.

prompt: Acetanilide (N-acetylaniline) is benzoylated with benzoyl chloride and AlCl3, and the product is hydrolyzed with NaOH in H2O. What is the final product?

choices.text: 4-Aminobenzophenone, p-H2NC6H4COC6H5
No product, because Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on amino-substituted rings
choices.why: They fail on free amines, but Friedel–Crafts alkylations and acylations of N-arylamides proceed normally.

choices.text: 3-Aminobenzophenone
choices.why: The amido group is ortho-, para-directing, and benzoylation occurs para to it.

choices.text: N-(4-Benzoylphenyl)acetamide, p-CH3CONHC6H4COC6H5
choices.why: That is the product before hydrolysis. NaOH and H2O then hydrolyze the amide to the free amine.

explanation: Friedel–Crafts alkylations and acylations of N-arylamides proceed normally. Benzoylation of acetanilide puts the benzoyl group para to the amido group, and hydrolysis then gives 4-aminobenzophenone in 80% yield.

prompt: In the synthesis of sulfanilamide, the last step hydrolyzes the acetamide group while the sulfonamide group survives. Why?

choices.text: Sulfonamides hydrolyze very slowly
The sulfonamide is formed only after the hydrolysis step
choices.why: The sulfonamide forms before the amide hydrolysis. It survives because sulfonamides hydrolyze very slowly.

choices.text: The AlCl3 catalyst protects the sulfonamide
choices.why: No AlCl3 is used. The selectivity comes from the slow hydrolysis of sulfonamides.

choices.text: The sulfonamide group is not attached to the ring
choices.why: The sulfonamide is on the ring, para to the amide. It survives because sulfonamides hydrolyze very slowly.

explanation: Sulfa drugs are made by chlorosulfonation of acetanilide, reaction of p-(N-acetylamino)benzenesulfonyl chloride with ammonia or another amine to give a sulfonamide, and hydrolysis of the amide. The amide can be hydrolyzed in the presence of the sulfonamide because sulfonamides hydrolyze very slowly.

prompt: Which sequence makes m-chloroaniline from benzene?

choices.text: HNO3, H2SO4; then Cl2, FeCl3; then SnCl2
Cl2, FeCl3; then HNO3, H2SO4; then SnCl2
choices.why: Chlorine is an ortho, para director, so nitrating chlorobenzene would not put the nitro group meta.

choices.text: HNO3, H2SO4; then SnCl2; then Cl2, FeCl3
choices.why: Reducing first gives the strongly activating, ortho-, para-directing amino group, so chlorine would not go meta.

choices.text: HNO3, H2SO4; then H2/PtO2; then (CH3CO)2O; then Cl2; then H2O, NaOH
choices.why: That is the route to p-chloroaniline: the acetamido group directs chlorine para.

explanation: The nitro group is a meta director, so chlorinate while it is still a nitro group and then reduce it: HNO3/H2SO4; Cl2/FeCl3; SnCl2 (Exercise 24.8.2c). Reducing first would give an amino group, which directs ortho and para.

prompt: N,N-Dimethylaniline is made from benzene by nitration (HNO3, H2SO4), reduction (H2/PtO2), and then alkylation with CH3Br. How many equivalents of CH3Br are used in the last step?
explanation: Aniline has two N–H hydrogens to replace with methyl groups, so 2 CH3Br are used: 1. HNO3, H2SO4; 2. H2/PtO2; 3. 2 CH3Br (Exercise 24.8.2a).

prompt: What forms when a primary arylamine reacts with nitrous acid, HNO2?

choices.text: An arenediazonium salt, ArN2+ X−
An aryl cation and nitrogen gas, N2
choices.why: Loss of N2 from an arenediazonium ion to give an aryl cation is disfavored, because the aryl cation is unstable.

choices.text: A nitroarene, ArNO2
choices.why: Nitroarenes come from nitration. Nitrous acid converts the –NH2 group into a diazonio group.

choices.text: An azo compound, Ar–N=N–Ar′
choices.why: Azo compounds form in a later step, when a diazonium salt couples with an activated ring.

explanation: Primary arylamines react with nitrous acid, HNO2, to yield stable arenediazonium salts, ArN2+ X−, a process called diazotization.

prompt: How do alkanediazonium ions, formed from alkylamines and nitrous acid, differ from arenediazonium ions?

choices.text: They lose N2 instantly to give carbocations, so they can't be isolated
They are more stable, so they can be stored
choices.why: That's reversed. Alkanediazonium ions are so reactive that they can't be isolated; arenediazonium salts are the stable ones.

choices.text: They don't form at all, because alkylamines don't react with nitrous acid
choices.why: Alkylamines do react with nitrous acid. The alkanediazonium products just can't be isolated.

choices.text: They couple with phenols to give azo dyes
choices.why: Diazonium coupling is a reaction of arenediazonium salts. Alkanediazonium ions lose N2 instantly.

explanation: Alkylamines also react with nitrous acid, but the alkanediazonium products are so reactive that they can't be isolated; they lose nitrogen instantly to yield carbocations. The analogous loss of N2 from an arenediazonium ion is disfavored by the instability of the aryl cation.

prompt: The section calls one route perhaps the single most versatile method of aromatic substitution, used to put groups such as –Br, –CN, or –OH onto a ring. Starting from the arene, how many steps does it have?
explanation: The sequence is (1) nitration, (2) reduction, (3) diazotization, and (4) nucleophilic substitution of the diazonio group: four steps.

prompt: p-Methylaniline is treated with HNO2 and H2SO4, and the diazonium salt is then treated with CuBr. What is the product?

choices.text: p-Bromotoluene
p-Bromoaniline
choices.why: The –NH2 group becomes the diazonio group, which is replaced. No nitrogen remains on the ring.

choices.text: o-Bromotoluene
choices.why: Bromine takes the place of the diazonio group, at the same position, para to the methyl group.

choices.text: p-Cresol (p-methylphenol)
choices.why: p-Cresol forms with Cu2O in aqueous Cu(NO3)2, not with CuBr.

explanation: Aryl chlorides and bromides are made by reaction of an arenediazonium salt with the corresponding copper(I) halide, CuX: the Sandmeyer reaction. Bromine replaces the diazonio group, giving p-bromotoluene. Aryl iodides are made with NaI, without a copper(I) salt.

prompt: Why is o-methylbenzoic acid made from o-methylaniline (diazotization, then CuCN, then H3O+) rather than by side-chain oxidation of o-xylene?

choices.text: Oxidizing o-xylene would oxidize both methyl groups
o-Xylene doesn't react with oxidizing agents
choices.why: It does react. The problem is that both methyl groups would be oxidized, not just one.

choices.text: Side-chain oxidation would move the group to the meta position
choices.why: Oxidation doesn't move substituents. It would turn both CH3 groups into carboxyl groups.

choices.text: The CuCN route adds two carbons to the ring
choices.why: CuCN adds one carbon, the nitrile carbon, which becomes the carboxyl carbon on hydrolysis.

explanation: Sandmeyer reaction of o-methylbenzenediazonium bisulfate with CuCN gives o-methylbenzonitrile, which is hydrolyzed to o-methylbenzoic acid. This product can't be made from o-xylene by the usual side-chain oxidation, because both methyl groups would be oxidized.

prompt: Which reagent converts an arenediazonium salt into a phenol?

choices.text: Cu2O in aqueous Cu(NO3)2
CuCN and KCN
choices.why: CuCN replaces the diazonio group with –CN, giving a nitrile, ArCN.

choices.text: H3PO2, hypophosphorous acid
choices.why: Hypophosphorous acid replaces the diazonio group with –H, giving an arene.

choices.text: CuCl, a copper(I) halide
choices.why: CuCl gives an aryl chloride by the Sandmeyer reaction.

explanation: A phenol is made by reaction of the arenediazonium salt with copper(I) oxide in aqueous copper(II) nitrate. This is especially useful because few other general methods exist for putting an –OH group onto an aromatic ring.

prompt: p-Methylaniline is diazotized with HNO2 and H2SO4, and the diazonium salt is treated with Cu2O in aqueous Cu(NO3)2. What percentage yield of p-cresol does the section report?
explanation: Replacing the diazonio group with –OH using copper(I) oxide in aqueous copper(II) nitrate gives p-cresol from p-methylaniline in 93% yield.

prompt: What does treating an arenediazonium salt with hypophosphorous acid, H3PO2, accomplish?

choices.text: It replaces the diazonio group with –H, removing the nitrogen from the ring
It replaces the diazonio group with –OH
choices.why: Phenols are made with Cu2O in aqueous Cu(NO3)2.

choices.text: It reduces the diazonium salt back to the arylamine
choices.why: H3PO2 replaces the whole diazonio group with hydrogen, giving an arene.

choices.text: It couples the diazonium ion with another ring to give an azo compound
choices.why: Coupling needs an activated ring such as a phenol or arylamine, not H3PO2.

explanation: Treating a diazonium salt with H3PO2 reduces it to an arene. This is used mainly when an amino group is put on a ring temporarily, for its directing effect, and then removed.

prompt: Why is 3,5-dibromotoluene made from p-toluidine (Br2, then diazotization, then H3PO2) instead of by direct bromination of toluene?

choices.text: Toluene itself would be brominated at positions 2 and 4 instead
Toluene doesn't react with Br2 and FeBr3 at all
choices.why: Toluene does react, but bromination occurs at positions 2 and 4, giving 2,4-dibromotoluene.

choices.text: Direct bromination gives 3,5-dibromotoluene too, but more slowly
choices.why: Direct bromination gives 2,4-dibromotoluene, not the 3,5 isomer.

choices.text: The amino group is needed in the final product
choices.why: The amino group is removed at the end with H3PO2. It is there only for its directing effect.

explanation: 3,5-Dibromotoluene can't be made by direct bromination of toluene, because reaction occurs at positions 2 and 4. Starting with p-toluidine, dibromination occurs ortho to the strongly directing amino group; diazotization followed by H3PO2 then removes the amino group.

prompt: By what kind of pathway do diazonio replacement reactions such as the Sandmeyer reaction occur?

choices.text: A radical pathway, by way of an aryl radical
A polar S_N2 pathway, with backside attack at the ring carbon
choices.why: These replacement reactions occur through radical rather than polar pathways.

choices.text: An S_N1 pathway through an aryl cation
choices.why: Forming an aryl cation is disfavored because the cation is unstable. The reactions go through aryl radicals.

choices.text: Electrophilic aromatic substitution by Cu+
choices.why: The diazonio group is replaced by way of an aryl radical, not by electrophilic attack on the ring.

explanation: Mechanistically, diazonio replacement reactions occur through radical rather than polar pathways. With a copper(I) compound, the arenediazonium ion is thought to be converted to an aryl radical plus copper(II), which then react to give the product and regenerate the copper(I) catalyst.

prompt: In planning a synthesis of m-hydroxyacetophenone from benzene, why does the acetyl group go on first?

choices.text: The acetyl group is a meta director, so the nitration that starts the –OH sequence then goes meta
The hydroxyl group is a meta director, so it can't go on first
choices.why: An –OH group is an ortho and para director. The acetyl group is the meta director.

choices.text: Friedel–Crafts acylation works only on rings that already carry an –OH group
choices.why: Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene itself gives acetophenone, the first intermediate.

choices.text: The –OH group can be put directly onto benzene with Cu2O
choices.why: Cu2O in aqueous Cu(NO3)2 replaces a diazonio group. The –OH must be introduced by nitration, reduction, diazotization, and replacement.

explanation: An acetyl group is a meta director while a hydroxyl group is an ortho and para director, so acetophenone is the immediate precursor. Benzene → acetophenone (CH3COCl, AlCl3), then nitration (meta), reduction, diazotization, and replacement of the diazonio group with –OH (Worked Example 24.8.1).

prompt: How many steps does the section's synthesis of m-hydroxyacetophenone from benzene use, counting the Friedel–Crafts acylation as the first?
explanation: Friedel–Crafts acylation gives acetophenone (1 step). The four-step sequence of nitration, reduction, diazotization, and diazonio replacement then introduces the –OH group meta to the acetyl group: 1 + 4 = 5 (Worked Example 24.8.1).

prompt: Benzenediazonium ion couples with phenol. Where on the phenol ring does reaction usually occur, and what is the product?

choices.text: At the para position, giving p-hydroxyazobenzene
At the meta position, giving m-hydroxyazobenzene
choices.why: The –OH group activates the ortho and para positions, and coupling usually occurs para.

choices.text: On the oxygen atom, giving an aryl ether
choices.why: Coupling is an electrophilic aromatic substitution on a ring carbon, usually the para carbon.

choices.text: At the ortho position, giving o-hydroxyazobenzene
choices.why: Reaction usually occurs at the para position.

explanation: Diazonium coupling reactions are typical electrophilic aromatic substitutions: the positively charged diazonium ion is the electrophile that reacts with the electron-rich ring of a phenol or arylamine, usually at the para position. Benzenediazonium ion and phenol give p-hydroxyazobenzene, orange crystals.

prompt: Why are azo compounds such as p-(dimethylamino)azobenzene brightly colored?

choices.text: Their extended conjugated π system absorbs visible light
They contain a positively charged nitrogen
choices.why: Azo compounds, Ar–N=N–Ar′, are neutral. Their color comes from extended conjugation.

choices.text: They contain copper left over from the coupling step
choices.why: No copper is used in diazonium coupling.

choices.text: Their N=N bond breaks when light strikes it
choices.why: The color comes from absorption of visible light by the extended conjugated π electron system.

explanation: Azo-coupled products are widely used as dyes for textiles because their extended conjugated π electron system absorbs in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum. p-(Dimethylamino)azobenzene, for instance, is a bright yellow compound once used to color margarine.

prompt: Which two partners couple to give p-(dimethylamino)azobenzene?

choices.text: Benzenediazonium ion and N,N-dimethylaniline
Benzenediazonium ion and phenol
choices.why: Phenol gives p-hydroxyazobenzene.

choices.text: Benzenediazonium ion and benzene
choices.why: Coupling needs an activated ring, such as a phenol or an arylamine. Benzene itself isn't activated.

choices.text: Benzenediazonium ion and aniline
choices.why: Aniline has no methyl groups on nitrogen, so the product would lack the dimethylamino group.

explanation: Benzenediazonium ion reacts with the activated ring of N,N-dimethylaniline at the para position, giving p-(dimethylamino)azobenzene. In Exercise 24.8.4 both partners come from benzene: nitration and SnCl2 reduction give aniline, part of which is methylated with 2 equivalents of CH3I and part diazotized with NaNO2 and H2SO4.
